title: Reading Input with cin and getline
summary: Read numbers, words, whole lines, and input of unknown length from standard input with std::cin and std::getline.
intro: Until now every program used data written in its code. Real programs read it: from a user, a file, or a judge feeding test cases. In C++ that is `std::cin` for values and `std::getline` for whole lines. From this lesson on, practices run once per test with different input, so your program has to work for all of them.

steps.title: Reading values with std::cin
steps.body:
`std::cin` from `<iostream>` reads from standard input, the text fed to your program. `std::cin >> x` skips any spaces, tabs, and newlines, then reads one token and converts it to the type of `x`.

```cpp
std::string name;
int age = 0;
double height = 0.0;
std::cin >> name >> age >> height;   // input: Ada 36 1.65
```

Chaining `>>` reads several values left to right. Whitespace between them does not matter, so `Ada 36 1.65` on one line and the same three values on three lines read the same way. A `std::string` read with `>>` stops at the first space, so it holds one word.

- Initialize every variable before reading into it. A read that fails at the end of input leaves the variable unchanged, and an uninitialized one would hold garbage.
- Never print a prompt such as `Enter your age:`. The checker compares all of stdout, so a prompt is wrong output.

`std::string` starts empty, so it needs no initializer.

example.title: Next birthday
example.prompt: Read a name and an age, then print the age the person turns next year.
example.explanation: The first `>>` skips nothing and reads `Ada` into `name`, stopping at the space. The second `>>` skips that space, reads `36`, and converts it to an `int`, so `age + 1` is real arithmetic. The program prints nothing before reading because a prompt would become part of the checked output.

practice.title: Order line
practice.prompt:
Read a product name, a quantity, and a unit price, then print the order line with its total.

1. Read a one-word `std::string` name, an `int` quantity, and a `double` price with one chained `std::cin` statement.
2. Compute the total as quantity times price.
3. Print `<quantity> x <name> = <total>` with the total to 2 decimal places.

Input:

```text
pen 3 1.50
```

Expected output:

```text
3 x pen = 4.50
```
hints: Declare a `std::string`, an `int`, and a `double`, each with an initial value, then read all three in one statement by chaining `>>`.
`quantity * price` mixes `int` and `double`, so the result is a `double`. The `std::fixed` and `std::setprecision(2)` already in the starter format it.

steps.title: Reading n values into a vector

example.title: Sum, min, and max
example.prompt: Read a count n and then n integers, and print their sum, minimum, and maximum.
example.explanation: The first read takes `5`. The loop then reads five more tokens, and it does not care that they sit on the next line because `>>` skips the newline. Only after all values are in the vector does the program compute: `std::accumulate` adds them from a start of `0`, and `*std::min_element` and `*std::max_element` read the smallest and largest. Those are safe here because n is at least 1, so the vector is not empty.

practice.title: Temperature report
practice.prompt:
Read a count n and then n temperatures, and print their average and how many were below zero.

1. Read `n`, then read `n` temperatures as `double` values into a `std::vector<double>`.
2. Compute the average of all temperatures.
3. Count the temperatures strictly below `0` (a reading of `0.0` does not count).
4. Print `average <value>` with 1 decimal place, then `below zero <count>` on the next line.

Input:

```text
5
-3.5 2.0 7.5 -1.0 4.0
```

Expected output:

```text
average 1.8
below zero 2
```

You can assume n is at least 1.
hints: `std::vector<double> temps(n);` makes n slots, and `std::cin >> temps[i]` fills each one.
After reading, loop once with a `double` sum and an `int` counter. `sum / n` is a `double` because `sum` is.

steps.title: Reading until the input ends

example.title: Count and sum
example.prompt: Read integers until the input ends, then print how many there were and their sum.
example.explanation: Each pass of the loop first tries to read. The four reads of `3`, `9`, `4`, and `1` succeed, so the body runs four times. The fifth read finds only the end of input, the stream turns `false`, and the loop exits without touching `count` or `sum`. No vector is needed because each value is used once and then forgotten.

practice.title: Longest word
practice.prompt:
Read words until the input ends, then print how many there were and the longest one.

1. Read one word at a time with `while (std::cin >> word)`.
2. Count every word.
3. Keep the longest word seen so far. On a tie keep the earlier word, so only replace it when the new word is strictly longer.
4. Print `count <n>`, then `longest <word>` on the next line.

Input:

```text
the quick brown fox jumps
```

Expected output:

```text
count 5
longest quick
```

The words may span several lines, and there is at least one word.
hints: The loop shape is the same as the example, with a `std::string` instead of an `int`.
Compare with `>`, not `>=`. Using `>=` would let a later word of the same length win the tie.

steps.title: Whole lines with std::getline

example.title: Long names
example.prompt: Read a minimum length, then full names one per line until the input ends, and print each name that has at least that many characters, with its length.
example.stdin:
12
Grace Hopper
Alan Turing
Ada Lovelace
Katherine Johnson
example.output:
Grace Hopper (12)
Ada Lovelace (12)
Katherine Johnson (17)
example.explanation: `std::cin >> minLength` reads `12` and stops before the newline. `std::ws` eats that newline, so the first `getline` starts at `Grace`. Each `getline` then reads one whole line, space included, which is why the lengths count the space. `Alan Turing` has 11 characters, so it is skipped. When no lines are left, `getline` turns the stream `false` and the loop ends. Without `>> std::ws` the first line read would be the empty rest of the `12` line. The same `>> std::ws` works before a loop that reads a known count of lines.

practice.title: Comment thread
practice.prompt:
Read a title line, a starting number, and then comment lines until the input ends, then print the title in uppercase and the comments numbered.

1. Read the whole first line as the title with `std::getline`.
2. Read the starting number with `>>`, then skip the leftover newline with `std::ws`.
3. Print the title in uppercase.
4. Read every remaining line with `while (std::getline(std::cin, comment))` and print it as `<number>. <comment>`, numbering from the starting number and adding 1 for each comment.

Input:

```text
Learn C++ fast
1
Great lesson!
Too short, more please
```

Expected output:

```text
LEARN C++ FAST
1. Great lesson!
2. Too short, more please
```

There may be no comment lines at all, and then only the title is printed.

tests.stdin:
Learn C++ fast
1
Great lesson!
Too short, more please
tests.output:
LEARN C++ FAST
1. Great lesson!
2. Too short, more please

tests.stdin:
Day 3 recap
11
See you tomorrow
ok
The getline part was tricky
tests.output:
DAY 3 RECAP
11. See you tomorrow
12. ok
13. The getline part was tricky

hints: The title comes first, so a plain `std::getline(std::cin, title)` reads it. Only the `>> number` read leaves a newline behind, so put `std::ws` right after it.
Uppercase in place with `for (char& c : title)` and `std::toupper(static_cast<unsigned char>(c))`, cast back to `char`.
Inside the `while` loop, print the current number with the comment, then increase it with `++number`.

recap:
- `std::cin >> x` skips whitespace and reads one token as the type of `x`. Chain `>>` to read several values.
- A `std::string` read with `>>` holds one word.
- Initialize variables before reading and never print prompts.
- Read a count `n`, then loop `n` times with `push_back`, or size the vector with `std::vector<int> v(n)` and read into `v[i]`.
- Read everything first, then process it.
- `while (std::cin >> x)` reads until the input ends, because the stream converts to `false` when a read fails.
- `std::getline(std::cin, line)` reads a whole line with its spaces.
- `>>` leaves the newline behind, so write `std::cin >> n >> std::ws` before a `getline`.
- `while (std::getline(std::cin, line))` reads every remaining line.
- `std::ios::sync_with_stdio(false);` speeds up large inputs.
